items.prompt:
(1) Which general property pair makes a metal useful for electrical wiring?
A. High density and scratch resistance
B. Thermal conduction and material brittleness
C. Low density and electrical insulation
D. Electrical conductivity and material ductility [1]

(2) Which diagram description best represents an alloy model?
A. A metallic array of identical atoms only
B. A mixture of separate unbonded gas atoms
C. Metallic array with different atom types
D. A regular array of positive and negative ions [1]

(3) How do most metals occur in ores?
A. Native metals mixed with sand
B. Chemically combined in mineral compounds
C. Separate atoms within inert minerals
D. Alloys separated by physical methods [1]

(4) Which pair can occur native?
A. Gold and platinum
B. Sodium and potassium
C. Aluminium and zinc
D. Calcium and magnesium [1]

(5) Which ore is associated with iron?
A. Galena
B. Haematite
C. Chalcopyrite
D. Bauxite [1]

(6) Which metal is obtained from galena?
A. Aluminium
B. Tin
C. Zinc
D. Lead [1]

(7) Why is an electric arc furnace suited to a supply of sorted steel scrap?
A. It removes carbon without supplying melting energy
B. It reduces fresh iron oxide using only electricity
C. It electrically melts scrap for controlled steel production
D. It melts scrap without needing composition control [1]

(8) Why is molten cryolite used with aluminium oxide in aluminium extraction?
A. It forms an aqueous oxide solution
B. It dissolves oxide at lower temperature
C. It chemically reduces aluminium ions itself
D. It blocks ions from the cathode [1]

(9) Why does recycling metals conserve ores?
A. Recycling reduces demand for ore extraction
B. Recycling rapidly renews the original ore deposit
C. Recycling makes every alloy suitable for any use
D. Recycling eliminates all processing energy requirements [1]

(10) Why are additions to steel controlled?
A. Composition must suit the intended properties
B. Extra carbon improves all steel properties
C. All added elements have identical effects
D. Steel must retain one molecular formula [1]

(11) Which pair names uses of zinc?
A. Electrical wiring and aircraft skins
B. Tin-plating and bronze
C. Glassmaking and paper bleaching
D. Galvanising and brass [1]

(12) Which is a syllabus use of uranium?
A. A catalyst in ammonia manufacture
B. A coating that protects iron from rust
C. Fuel in nuclear power stations
D. An alloying metal used to make brass [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) D. Electrical conductivity and material ductility. A wire must carry current and be drawn into shape.
Distractor explanations: A: Neither density nor scratch resistance establishes current conduction and drawability. B: Brittleness is unsuitable for drawing wires; thermal conduction is not the required electrical property. C: Electrical insulation prevents the wire from carrying current.

(2) C. Metallic array with different atom types. An alloy mixes elements in a metallic material.
Distractor explanations: A: Identical atoms only represent a pure metal rather than an alloy. B: An alloy is a condensed metallic material, not separate gas atoms. D: Alternating opposite ions represent ionic bonding, not an alloy.

(3) B. Chemically combined in mineral compounds. Most occur combined with other elements.
Distractor explanations: A: Native occurrence is restricted to sufficiently unreactive metals, not most ores. C: The metals are chemically combined, not free separate atoms in inert material. D: Ores are typically mineral compounds, not ready-made metallic alloys.

(4) A. Gold and platinum. Low reactivity allows native occurrence.
Distractor explanations: B: Sodium and potassium are too reactive to persist native under ordinary conditions. C: Aluminium and zinc normally occur in compounds. D: Calcium and magnesium normally occur in compounds.

(5) B. Haematite. Haematite contains iron oxide.
Distractor explanations: A: Galena is a lead ore. C: Chalcopyrite is a copper-bearing ore. D: Bauxite is an aluminium ore.

(6) D. Lead. Galena is PbS.
Distractor explanations: A: Galena is lead sulfide, not an aluminium compound. B: Galena is lead sulfide, not a tin compound. C: Galena is lead sulfide, not a zinc compound.

(7) C. It electrically melts scrap for controlled steel production. Electrical heating melts the scrap feed.
Distractor explanations: A: Energy is required to melt the scrap. B: This describes neither the scrap feed nor its melting process; oxide reduction needs a reducing route. D: Composition must be controlled to obtain the required steel properties.

(8) B. It dissolves oxide at lower temperature. The molten mixture permits electrolysis at lower temperature than pure alumina.
Distractor explanations: A: The electrolyte is molten, not aqueous. C: Electrical reduction produces aluminium; cryolite is not the reducing agent. D: The molten electrolyte must allow ions to reach electrodes.

(9) A. Recycling reduces demand for ore extraction. Reusing material reduces fresh extraction.
Distractor explanations: B: Recycling does not regenerate an ore deposit. C: Alloys have different compositions and cannot all substitute for each other. D: Collection, sorting and melting still consume energy.

(10) A. Composition must suit the intended properties. Useful properties depend on controlled composition.
Distractor explanations: B: More carbon can increase hardness while reducing ductility; it does not improve every property. C: Different alloying elements have different effects. D: Steel is an alloy mixture, not a substance with one molecular formula.

(11) D. Galvanising and brass. Zinc coats steel and combines with copper in brass.
Distractor explanations: A: These are common copper/aluminium uses, not the stated zinc pair. B: Tin-plating and bronze are associated with tin. C: Neither is the specified zinc use pair.

(12) C. Fuel in nuclear power stations. Uranium provides nuclear fuel.
Distractor explanations: A: The Haber process uses iron, not uranium, as its catalyst. B: Zinc is used for galvanising iron. D: Brass contains copper and zinc, not uranium.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option D (1). D. Electrical conductivity and material ductility. A wire must carry current and be drawn into shape. Distractor explanations: A: Neither density nor scratch resistance establishes current conduction and drawability. B: Brittleness is unsuitable for drawing wires; thermal conduction is not the required electrical property. C: Electrical insulation prevents the wire from carrying current. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 2: Correct option C (1). C. Metallic array with different atom types. An alloy mixes elements in a metallic material. Distractor explanations: A: Identical atoms only represent a pure metal rather than an alloy. B: An alloy is a condensed metallic material, not separate gas atoms. D: Alternating opposite ions represent ionic bonding, not an alloy. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 3: Correct option B (1). B. Chemically combined in mineral compounds. Most occur combined with other elements. Distractor explanations: A: Native occurrence is restricted to sufficiently unreactive metals, not most ores. C: The metals are chemically combined, not free separate atoms in inert material. D: Ores are typically mineral compounds, not ready-made metallic alloys. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 4: Correct option A (1). A. Gold and platinum. Low reactivity allows native occurrence. Distractor explanations: B: Sodium and potassium are too reactive to persist native under ordinary conditions. C: Aluminium and zinc normally occur in compounds. D: Calcium and magnesium normally occur in compounds. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 5: Correct option B (1). B. Haematite. Haematite contains iron oxide. Distractor explanations: A: Galena is a lead ore. C: Chalcopyrite is a copper-bearing ore. D: Bauxite is an aluminium ore. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 6: Correct option D (1). D. Lead. Galena is PbS. Distractor explanations: A: Galena is lead sulfide, not an aluminium compound. B: Galena is lead sulfide, not a tin compound. C: Galena is lead sulfide, not a zinc compound. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 7: Correct option C (1). C. It electrically melts scrap for controlled steel production. Electrical heating melts the scrap feed. Distractor explanations: A: Energy is required to melt the scrap. B: This describes neither the scrap feed nor its melting process; oxide reduction needs a reducing route. D: Composition must be controlled to obtain the required steel properties. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 8: Correct option B (1). B. It dissolves oxide at lower temperature. The molten mixture permits electrolysis at lower temperature than pure alumina. Distractor explanations: A: The electrolyte is molten, not aqueous. C: Electrical reduction produces aluminium; cryolite is not the reducing agent. D: The molten electrolyte must allow ions to reach electrodes. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 9: Correct option A (1). A. Recycling reduces demand for ore extraction. Reusing material reduces fresh extraction. Distractor explanations: B: Recycling does not regenerate an ore deposit. C: Alloys have different compositions and cannot all substitute for each other. D: Collection, sorting and melting still consume energy. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 10: Correct option A (1). A. Composition must suit the intended properties. Useful properties depend on controlled composition. Distractor explanations: B: More carbon can increase hardness while reducing ductility; it does not improve every property. C: Different alloying elements have different effects. D: Steel is an alloy mixture, not a substance with one molecular formula. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 11: Correct option D (1). D. Galvanising and brass. Zinc coats steel and combines with copper in brass. Distractor explanations: A: These are common copper/aluminium uses, not the stated zinc pair. B: Tin-plating and bronze are associated with tin. C: Neither is the specified zinc use pair. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 12: Correct option C (1). C. Fuel in nuclear power stations. Uranium provides nuclear fuel. Distractor explanations: A: The Haber process uses iron, not uranium, as its catalyst. B: Zinc is used for galvanising iron. D: Brass contains copper and zinc, not uranium. No mark for more than one selected option.

items.prompt:
(a) State which is more reactive, magnesium or copper. [1]

(b) Describe the two visible changes in this original supplied record: magnesium is placed in blue CuSO4 solution; a reddish-brown coating appears on the strip and the solution becomes paler. Relate them to the displacement products. [2]

(c) Explain why an intact paint coating prevents iron rusting under ordinary moist-air conditions. [2]

(d) Explain why a scratch through a zinc coating need not cause immediate rusting of the exposed iron when surrounding zinc remains electrically connected in a moist environment. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Magnesium.

(b) Copper metal forms the reddish-brown coating, while removal of Cu²⁺ makes the blue solution fade.

(c) Paint blocks water and oxygen from reaching iron, preventing the simultaneous contact needed for rusting.

(d) Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it oxidises preferentially and provides sacrificial protection to the exposed iron.
marking_guidance: Part a: Magnesium (1).
Part b: Copper coating forms (1).
Part b: Blue solution fades as Cu²⁺ is removed (1).
Part c: Excludes water/oxygen (1).
Part c: Prevents required rusting conditions (1).
Part d: Zinc more reactive (1).
Part d: Preferential oxidation of zinc (1).
Part d: Sacrificial protection of exposed iron (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Plan a teacher-supervised comparison of magnesium and zinc reacting with excess dilute hydrochloric acid to investigate relative reactivity. Include controls, gas measurements and the comparison used for a conclusion. No flames are permitted near the hydrogen-generating apparatus. [6]

(b) Calculate the average magnesium gas-production rate over 0–30 s. Original synthetic gas data: time / s 0, 10, 20, 30; Mg gas / cm³ 0, 12, 22, 30; Zn gas / cm³ 0, 5, 9, 12. Exposed areas, acid concentration and volume, and starting temperature are matched; acid is in excess. [2]

(c) State the two measured quantities needed to compare gas-production rates in these trials. Original synthetic gas data: time / s 0, 10, 20, 30; Mg gas / cm³ 0, 12, 22, 30; Zn gas / cm³ 0, 5, 9, 12. Exposed areas, acid concentration and volume, and starting temperature are matched; acid is in excess. [2]

(d) Explain how oxide coatings could distort the rate comparison, and give a practical improvement to surface preparation. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Use the same dilute HCl concentration, volume and temperature in separate comparable flasks. Match exposed strip areas and clean surfaces consistently. Collect hydrogen through a leak-free delivery tube into a freely moving gas syringe, starting timing at mixing. Record gas volume at equal time intervals and repeat each metal. Compare early gradients or average volume change per equal interval; a larger rate supports greater reactivity under these controlled conditions. Keep acid in excess and hydrogen away from flames; do not test sodium or potassium with acid.

(b) Average rate=(30−0)/(30−0)=1.00 cm³/s.

(c) Elapsed time and gas volume.

(d) An oxide layer can limit acid contact and make the apparent reaction slower. Clean the metal surfaces consistently before testing so unequal coatings are less likely to control the comparison.
marking_guidance: Part a: Same acid concentration (1).
Part a: Same acid volume and temperature (1).
Part a: Matched exposed metal area (1).
Part a: Safe workable gas collection (1).
Part a: Gas volume measured against time (1).
Part a: Compare rates to support relative-reactivity conclusion (1). Accept equivalent controlled safe collection; maximum six marks.
Part b: Volume change divided by elapsed time (1).
Part b: 1.00 cm³/s (1); accept 0.98–1.02 from allowed readings.
Part c: Time (1).
Part c: Gas volume (1).
Part d: Coating limits contact and alters apparent rate (1).
Part d: Consistent surface cleaning (1).
